Rail & roads · Zambia · Railway strips and road reserves

Structures and earthworks along rail and road reserves in Zambia

A dated register of the structures and works inside your railway strip or road reserve, each measured from the centreline or reserve boundary you supply, recorded before rehabilitation starts and compared at every later survey. For railway and road authorities, the engineers and contractors rebuilding cross-border corridors, and the ESIA and RAP teams working alongside them. A person reviews every result.

Send us your reserve file See sample outputs

The problem, in your words

What stands in the reserve before the works start

Tanzania-Zambia Railway Act, s.62

“Nothing may be built on the railway strip.”

“Except with the written permission of the Authority, a person shall not erect any building or structure or execute any works on the railway strip” (Tanzania-Zambia Railway Act, s.62). Unauthorised works can be ordered removed or modified within 30 days, after which the Authority may do the work and recover the cost.

Rehabilitation

“The corridor is being rebuilt.”

Zambia’s railway to the Indian Ocean was placed under a concession to rehabilitate, modernise and operate its freight services in September 2025, and rail links across the region are attracting lender finance. Rehabilitation brings works footprints, access roads, borrow pits and camps, and a record of what stood in the reserve before they started.

Cut-off dates

“We need a baseline before the census.”

Where rehabilitation or widening affects homes, fields or businesses, the resettlement plan fixes a cut-off date. A dated register of the structures inside the reserve on that date supports the census, and re-surveys show what appears later.

Railways Act (Cap. 453)

“Signals, crossings and fire risk.”

For the Zambia Railways network, the Railways Act lets a railway company seek a High Court order for the removal of a building that obscures a signal or endangers rail services (s.14(3)), defines a firebreak at least 10 m wide from the railway land boundary, and excludes liability for fire damage to buildings within 60 m of the rails (s.69(1)).

Who this is for

  • Railway and road authorities, and their land and property teams
  • Engineers and contractors on rehabilitation and upgrading projects
  • Concessionaires and their owner’s engineers
  • ESIA and RAP consultants
  • Lenders’ environmental and social advisers
  • Road-fund and programme implementation units

Reserve baselines before rehabilitation

A register of what stands in the reserve, at the widths in your records

We buffer the railway or road you supply in its UTM zone, from the centreline or the reserve boundary, at the widths in your records, and list each structure the review confirms with its distance, its band, its chainage and its coordinates. Each 500 m stretch is rated high, medium or low for encroachment density by a count rule, so your land team knows where the reserve is most built up. It is not a safety rating.

We have not confirmed a width for the Tanzania-Zambia railway strip or the road-reserve widths in the Public Roads Act, so every register states the widths you supplied and where they came from. The same survey can add the other distances that matter along a line of rail: the 100 m from any railway track within which a mining-right holder needs the railway administration’s consent (Minerals Regulation Commission Act 2024, s.35(1)(d)), and the 60 m and 10 m distances in the Railways Act.

Before rehabilitation, the baseline records the reserve as the works found it: structures with reviewer categories such as main building, outbuilding or under construction, tracks and informal crossings across the line, cleared ground and existing borrow pits. Once a cut-off date is set, the same register supports the resettlement census.

What you receive

  • A reserve register: ID, distance, band, chainage and coordinates
  • A density rating for each 500 m stretch, and a ranked list
  • Reviewer categories for each structure
  • Tracks and worn paths across the reserve
  • A dated baseline for the cut-off date
  • A PDF report and GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers

Widths as supplied

We measure at the widths you give us. We do not set or verify statutory reserve widths, and the register is not a land survey.

During the works

Construction progress and change along the corridor

Construction and earthworks progress

Dated drone orthophotos and elevation models compared side by side, with maps of where ground has been cut or filled between visits, subject to the approvals each operation requires. Not a certified survey or a valuation.

New structures in the reserve

New and removed structures between dated surveys, flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, with before-and-after views, so the reserve does not fill up again behind the works.

Camps, borrow pits and access roads

Borrow pits, spoil, laydown areas and new access tracks mapped between dates, and revegetation of closed borrow pits tracked afterwards.

After handover, re-surveys on the schedule you agree show what has appeared in the reserve since, with a notice after each one. Along long roads and railways the same work flags historically flooded and low-lying stretches and drainage crossings, for maintenance planning. See change detection and terrain and flood screening.

Road reserves

Road reserves and lender-financed road programmes

Road reserves fall under the Public Roads Act 2002, amended in 2022 and 2026. We did not retrieve its reserve widths, so every road register uses the widths in your records and says so. Lender-financed road programmes bring environmental and social standards with them, and where a lender applies IFC Performance Standard 5, anyone affected by widening or realignment is counted against a cut-off date.

For a road, we buffer the centreline or reserve boundary you supply, list each structure inside the reserve and in a band beyond it, and flag new structures and cleared ground between dated surveys. Where a road is being widened, a register of the structures along each side, with reviewer categories, gives the RAP team a dated starting point, and route options for a realignment can be compared by the structures each would affect.

Near roads, drones need care

Part 18 bars drone flights over, along or within 50 m of a public road without specific approval or a road closure, and take-off and landing on public roads is reserved to civil defence and law enforcement. Satellite work needs neither.

Drone law in Zambia

How it works

From reserve file to reviewed register

  1. Scope

    You send the route or reserve boundary, the widths in your records, the stretches being rehabilitated and the date the record must reflect. We agree the bands, imagery and deliverables in a written proposal.

  2. Screen from satellite

    Structures, tracks and works are mapped along the whole reserve from dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or the orthophotos you hold.

  3. Review

    A person checks every result; each structure is measured, banded and rated.

  4. Deliver and repeat

    The report and GIS layers go to the contacts you name. Re-surveys and drone progress surveys follow the schedule you set.

More on the global rail and roads overview, the methodology and imagery and data sources.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Map structures, tracks, cleared ground and works visible from the air
  • Measure each structure from the centreline or reserve boundary you supply
  • Flag change between dated surveys, confirmed by a reviewer
  • Compare works between drone surveys, where flown

What we don’t do

  • Set, verify or survey statutory reserve widths
  • Inspect track, bridges or pavements
  • Identify, count or follow people
  • Decide whether a structure has permission or must move

Also useful

Route & site selection

Structure counts along alternative alignments or across candidate sites, so land impact is weighed before a route is fixed.

Frequently asked questions

How wide is the railway strip?

The Tanzania-Zambia Railway Act prohibits building on the “railway strip” without the Authority’s written permission. We have not confirmed a width for the railway strip, so we measure from the reserve boundary or centreline you supply, at the widths in your own records, and can add the 100 m band within which a mining-right holder needs the railway administration’s consent, or the 60 m and 10 m distances in the Railways Act, as further bands.

Which road-reserve widths do you use?

The ones you supply. Road-reserve widths come from the Public Roads Act and the road authority’s own records, so send the reserve polygons or the width for each road class and we report each structure’s distance and band. Up to six widths can be reported in one survey.

Do you decide which structures must move?

No. We record what stands where and when it first appears in the imagery. Whether a structure has the railway or road authority’s permission, predates the reserve or has to move is for the authority, the owner and, if it comes to that, the courts. The register gives them a dated, located list to work from.

Can the register support a rehabilitation programme's cut-off date?

Yes. A dated record of the structures inside the reserve and the works footprint on the cut-off date supports the census and asset inventory, and re-surveys show what has appeared since. It does not replace the census, and categories do not establish use, ownership or value.

Can you track construction progress along the line?

From dated drone orthophotos and elevation models we compare works between visits, with maps of where ground has been cut or filled, subject to the ZCAA approvals and Zambia Air Force clearance each operation requires. Drone flights over, along or within 50 m of a public road need specific approval or a road closure. It is not a certified survey or a quantity surveyor’s valuation.

Can a drone fly along a railway or over a bridge?

Only within the ZCAA’s rules, and some crossings need more. The consolidated Protected Places and Areas Act prints orders that make land within 0.8045 km of the Kafue road and rail bridges and of the Luangwa Bridge protected areas (whether each is still in force is for Zambian counsel), and the State Security Act treats roads, railways and bridges as necessary services. Satellite work needs no flight; drone work near a bridge or rail installation is planned with the authority concerned.

Send us your reserve file

The route or reserve boundary (KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage), the reserve widths in your records, the stretches being rehabilitated and the date the record must reflect. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
